strengths: The paper addresses a clear gap in the model soups literature: extending soups to self-supervised ingredients, and is the first to show LMC can hold between ingredients trained with different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR), which is a genuinely novel empirical finding.

The experimental scope is broad: ImageNet with multiple shifted/robustness test sets (ImageNet-C, LAION-C, ImageNet-A/R/V2/ReaL/HR), 21-task VTAB transfer with a custom mini-VTAB-C corruption benchmark, and a second stock (Franca) to show generality.

The proposed 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline is a fair and well-matched control that isolates the specific contribution of mixing across differing SSL runs (not just having more/longer training), strengthening the causal claims.

The additional contributions (Self-Seasoning for label-free mixture selection, combination with test-time adaptation, demonstration on an alternate stock) show reasonable exploration of the idea's implications and robustness of the finding across settings.

The presentation with the soup/ingredient/stock analogy and diagrams (Figs. 1, 3) clearly communicates the relationship to prior work (Model Soups, Ratatouille) and precisely formalizes the method with an explicit equation.
Reasonably thorough implementation details are provided in the appendix (hyperparameter sweeps, optimizer settings, augmentation, SSL configurations), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The reported gains from Self-Souping (excluding the shift-aware inter-training experiment) are frequently very small (e.g., ~+1% on ImageNet-C, +0.4% on LAION-C, and often <1% on VTAB), and no statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, making it hard to know whether these differences are meaningful versus noise from a single run per configuration.

The headline +3.5%/+7% robustness gains (§4.3) rely on inter-training directly on the (unlabeled) target corrupted distribution, which is a much stronger and less general setup than the other experiments; this is somewhat conflated in the abstract with the more modest 'algorithm diversity' gains, potentially overstating the generality of the core Self-Soupervision idea.

Only 3 SSL algorithms (one per family) and a limited/small-scale experimental regime (ViT-B, short inter-training schedules of 5-10 epochs or 10-100K steps, small subsets like mini-VTAB with 1K samples) are used; it is unclear whether findings generalize to longer training, larger models, or other SSL methods, and the paper's own limitations section concedes this without providing supporting ablations.

The comparison in Table 1/2 selects 'best ingredient' and 'greedy search' based on ImageNet-Val accuracy, which can make the reported metric not the best possible result for other test sets (acknowledged in text), complicating fair comparison across methods and potentially underselling or overselling different baselines inconsistently.

The Self-Seasoning results (Table 5, §4.5) are mixed at best: it is only the best method on 4/21 tasks and can substantially underperform supervised seasoning and even the best single ingredient on several structured tasks (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs 33.7, dSpr-Loc-X 4.1 vs 11.6), which somewhat undercuts the claim that Self-Seasoning is broadly 'competitive.'

The relationship to model merging/multi-task SSL/domain adaptation is discussed only qualitatively; no quantitative comparison against any of these alternative approaches (e.g., TIES-merging, joint multi-task SSL) is provided, leaving open whether the specific 'separate inter-train then average' recipe is actually preferable to these alternatives in practice.
Some data/code links in the appendix (§C) appear to be placeholders ('Data.' / 'Code.' with no actual content), raising concerns about reproducibility support at submission time.

strengths: The core idea—extending model soups to self-supervised ingredients so that soups can be made without labels—is a reasonable and underexplored extension of the Model Soups / Ratatouille lineage, and the paper provides a clean formalization (Eq. 2) relating it to prior work.

The demonstration that linear mode connectivity can hold between ingredients fine-tuned from fundamentally different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR) is a genuinely novel empirical observation (Fig. 2) that was not previously shown in the souping literature.

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad: ImageNet plus 7 additional test sets, ImageNet-C/LAION-C corruption robustness, 21 VTAB tasks with a custom mini-VTAB-C corruption suite, and an additional stock (Franca) to check generality.

The paper introduces a fair and well-motivated baseline ("continued SSL + supervised soup") that matches the search/compute budget of the proposed method, which strengthens the comparison against simply conflating gains from extra training with gains from souping per se.
Self-Seasoning (unsupervised mixture-coefficient optimization via kNN entropy minimization) is a creative extension that attempts to make the entire pipeline label-free, including the mixing step.
weaknesses: Many of the reported gains are marginal and likely within noise: e.g., Table 1 shows Self-Soup beating baselines by ~0.1-0.3 points on most ImageNet variants, and Table 4's VTAB gains are frequently <1 point. No seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere in the paper, making it impossible to assess whether these small differences are reliable or artifacts of a single run.

The headline large gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C in §4.3) crucially depend on access to unlabeled data from the exact test/shift distribution at inter-training time — a strong and somewhat unrealistic assumption for genuine distribution-shift robustness, and this caveat is only briefly acknowledged in the Limitations paragraph.

Self-Seasoning's results in Table 5 are inconsistent and in several cases substantially worse than the uniform mix or best ingredient (e.g., Clevr-Count drops from 73.2/74.3 to 17.5, dSpr-Loc-X/Y/Ori also degrade sharply), undermining the claim that it is a reliable, generally competitive unsupervised mixing method rather than a sometimes-helpful heuristic that overfits to kNN entropy in a way misaligned with downstream accuracy.

Scale and scope of experiments are limited: inter-training runs are short (5 epochs / 10K-100K steps rather than the hundreds of epochs typical for realistic SSL pretraining), only a single architecture (ViT-B) and only 3 SSL algorithms/families are tested, and VTAB evaluation uses a 1K-sample "mini-VTAB" subset rather than the standard full benchmark, which limits comparability with the broader transfer-learning literature and the generality of conclusions.

Several SSL/training hyperparameters are explicitly stated as "chosen arbitrarily" and "not tuned" (Appendix B), which raises reproducibility and robustness concerns — it is unclear whether the reported effects would hold under different (equally defensible) hyperparameter choices.

The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is essentially Model Ratatouille's inter-train-then-fine-tune-then-mix recipe with the inter-training loss swapped from supervised to self-supervised, and the formal contribution (Eq. 2) is a direct notational substitution rather than a new algorithmic mechanism.
No code or data links are resolved in the submitted version (Appendix C placeholders are empty), making independent reproduction currently impossible to verify.

Comparisons are restricted to simple baselines (plain fine-tuning, uniform/greedy supervised soup, continued SSL + soup); no comparison to other robustness-oriented adaptation strategies beyond a single TTA method (SAR), and no analysis of computational/training cost trade-offs relative to the gains achieved.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual extension of model soups to self-supervised learning (SSL), filling a real gap since prior soup methods require labels at every stage.

Novel empirical finding that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold between ingredients trained with fundamentally different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR), which is a genuinely interesting and previously unreported result.
Fair baseline design: the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline matches the search/development cost of Self-Soupervision, making comparisons more credible than against naive baselines.

Broad experimental coverage: ImageNet with multiple OOD/shifted test sets, VTAB with 21 tasks and corruption variants, interaction with test-time adaptation (SAR), and generalization to an alternate stock (Franca), suggesting the approach is not overly brittle to a single setup.
Introduces Self-Seasoning, a label-free mixing procedure based on entropy minimization over nearest-neighbor predictions, extending the applicability of soup mixing to settings without any labels.
The paper is clearly written with helpful diagrams (Figs. 1, 3) that precisely delineate how Self-Soupervision differs from Model Soups and Model Ratatouille.
Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations (e.g., large gains require unlabeled target/shift data; only 3 SSL families tested).
weaknesses: Many reported gains are small (e.g., +0.3-1% in Tables 1 and 4) and no error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether these differences are statistically meaningful versus noise from a single run.

VTAB experiments use a reduced 'mini-VTAB' with only 1K train/test subsets per task, which could introduce substantial evaluation noise, especially given the already-small absolute gains being claimed as meaningful.

SSL algorithmic hyperparameters (e.g., masking ratio, temperature, local/global loss choice) are explicitly described as 'chosen arbitrarily' (Appendix B) and not tuned per baseline, raising concerns about whether comparisons across methods are fully fair or whether tuning could change relative rankings.

The headline large gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) come specifically from the setting where unlabeled target/shift distribution data is available for inter-training, which is a somewhat expected outcome of adapting to the test distribution rather than a surprising benefit of the souping mechanism itself; the paper could more directly disentangle how much of the gain is from 'souping' per se versus simply having access to in-domain unlabeled data.

In Table 5 (Self-Seasoning), the method occasionally underperforms the best single ingredient and even the uniform mix on several tasks (e.g., Pets, Sun397, Clevr-Count, dSpr-Loc-Y, sNORB-Elev), somewhat weakening the claim that Self-Seasoning is reliably competitive.
Limited diversity in SSL methods examined (3 algorithms, mostly MAE-centric) restricts how strongly the 'countless SSL algorithms' claim in the abstract can be generalized from the evidence given.

The theoretical or mechanistic explanation for why LMC holds across such different SSL losses is not explored beyond the empirical demonstration, leaving the central surprising finding somewhat unexplained.

strengths: The paper presents a natural and well-motivated generalization of model soups to the self-supervised setting, and is the first to empirically demonstrate that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold across ingredients trained with fundamentally different SSL losses (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA), which is a genuinely novel empirical finding.

The experimental scope is broad: ImageNet and its many shifted test sets (ReaL, V2, HR, A, R, C), LAION-C, and 21 VTAB tasks with a custom mini-VTAB-C benchmark, giving reasonably comprehensive coverage of the claims.

The paper includes well-designed, fair baselines (e.g., 'continued SSL + supervised soup') that control for search/development cost, which strengthens the claim that gains come specifically from souping across differing SSL runs rather than merely from extra training.

The proposed Self-Seasoning method, which mixes purely self-supervised ingredients without any labels via kNN-entropy minimization, is a creative and practically useful contribution for low-label regimes, and is empirically shown to be competitive with labeled seasoning.

The paper provides substantial reproducibility detail (training hyperparameters, learning-rate sweeps, code snippet for Self-Seasoning, appendix ablations with alternate augmentations and an alternate stock), and an honest limitations section.

The demonstrated robustness gains under distribution shift (particularly inter-training on corrupted/test-like unlabeled data before fine-tuning) are the paper's most compelling and practically significant results (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C).
weaknesses: Many of the reported gains are quite small (often <1%) on the primary in-distribution benchmarks (ImageNet-Val, VTAB clean accuracy), and the practical significance of these modest gains versus added SSL inter-training compute is not fully quantified against increased training cost.

Results are largely reported as single-run numbers without confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess whether the (frequently small) differences between soup types are robust or within noise, especially given the fine granularity of some tables (e.g., differences of 0.1-0.3%).

The core methodological contribution is conceptually a fairly direct combination of existing ideas (Model Soups + Model Ratatouille's inter-training scheme, substituting SSL losses for supervised losses), so the technical novelty is more in the empirical demonstration than in new algorithmic machinery.

Generalization across architectures/stocks is only lightly tested (one additional Franca stock ablation with 2 SSL algorithms), leaving open how well the findings transfer beyond ViT-B/MAE-style initializations.

The few-shot Self-Seasoning results (Table 9, Fig. 4) show that its advantage over plain fine-tuning vanishes or reverses as N grows past a few hundred samples, especially on specialized/structured VTAB tasks, which somewhat narrows the claimed practical utility to a fairly specific low-data regime that is not strongly emphasized in the main text.

The mini-VTAB/mini-VTAB-C subsets (1K train/test) and the 15-corruption synthetic shift construction are custom benchmarks without external validation, which could affect the generality of the transfer/robustness conclusions in §4.4.

The paper's discussion of *why* LMC holds across differently-trained SSL ingredients is largely empirical/observational; there is no theoretical or mechanistic analysis explaining this surprising phenomenon, which is flagged as a novel finding but left unexplained.

strengths: The paper tackles a reasonable open question: can model soups be made without supervised labels, extending the Model Soup / Model Ratatouille line of work to self-supervised inter-training.
Broad experimental sweep: ImageNet and its many test variants (ReaL, V2, HR, A, R, C), LAION-C, 21 VTAB tasks with a custom mini-VTAB-C corruption suite, and a few-shot seasoning study.

The demonstration that linear mode connectivity can hold between ingredients trained with fundamentally different SSL objectives (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA) is an interesting empirical observation not previously shown.

Self-Seasoning (unsupervised mixture-coefficient learning via kNN entropy minimization) is a reasonably novel practical contribution that removes the need for even few-shot labels when mixing SSL-only ingredients.
Reasonably detailed appendix with training configurations, which aids reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: Most reported gains are very small (often 0.1–0.9 percentage points) and no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere in the main tables, making it impossible to judge whether the claimed improvements of Self-Soup over the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline (which is itself a strong, closely related ablation) are statistically meaningful or within run-to-run noise.

The headline large gains (+3.5% ImageNet-C, +7% LAION-C, §4.3) come from inter-training directly on unlabeled samples from the same corruption distribution as the test set (disjoint but same corruption types/severity). This is closer to a form of distribution-specific test-time/domain adaptation than general-purpose robustness improvement, and the practical availability of such matched unlabeled shift data is a strong and somewhat unrealistic assumption that is not sufficiently flagged as limiting the generality of the headline numbers.

The core technical contribution is a fairly straightforward generalization of existing work (Model Soups + Model Ratatouille + continued SSL), mainly substituting supervised inter-training with SSL losses; the formal framework (Eq. 2) is a simple composition of previously known components rather than a new mechanism.

Many SSL algorithmic hyperparameters (masking ratio, temperature, λ for LeJEPA, etc.) are explicitly stated to be 'chosen arbitrarily' with claims that 'different choices achieve the same results'—this is asserted without evidence (no ablation table) and raises concerns about the robustness/reproducibility of the reported numbers to these choices.

VTAB evaluation uses a non-standard, self-constructed 'mini-VTAB' with 1K-sample subsets and a custom corruption suite (mini-VTAB-C), which deviates from established protocols and makes it hard to compare against prior VTAB literature or judge whether results generalize to the full benchmark.

In several tables (e.g., Table 1, Table 4) the proposed Self-Soup is not uniformly best; the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline wins or ties on multiple metrics (e.g., IN-HR, IN-A, several VTAB structured tasks), undermining the strength of the central claim that differing in SSL algorithm specifically (rather than just adding an SSL inter-training stage) is the source of benefit.

Self-Seasoning is only competitive with fine-tuning in a narrow regime (<500 labeled samples, natural tasks only); for specialized/structured VTAB tasks and larger N, fine-tuning substantially outperforms both seasoning variants (Table 9, Figure 4), limiting the practical significance of this contribution.

The paper only seriously explores one primary stock (MAE ViT-B); the secondary stock (Franca) experiment is minimal (2 ingredients, 2 metrics) and insufficient to support claims of general applicability across architectures/pretraining schemes.

Computational cost of the proposed pipeline (multiple SSL inter-trainings × multiple fine-tunings per configuration) is substantial but not clearly quantified or compared against baselines in terms of actual compute/GPU-hours, making the accuracy-vs-cost trade-off hard to assess despite the paper's claims about 'equal search cost' being only asserted, not empirically measured.

strengths: Clear and genuinely novel conceptual contribution: the paper formalizes a generalization of model soups (and Model Ratatouille) to self-supervised inter-training, removing the dependency on labeled auxiliary data at the inter-training stage. The formalism in Eq. 2 and Fig. 1/3 cleanly situates the method relative to prior soup variants.

The central empirical claim that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold between ingredients trained with fundamentally different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA) is an interesting and, to my knowledge, previously unestablished finding (Fig. 2), and is a nice addition to the broader LMC literature.

Breadth of experiments is commendable: ImageNet robustness benchmarks (ImageNet-C, LAION-C, ImageNet-A/R/V2/ReaL/HR), transfer to 21 VTAB tasks with a custom corrupted variant (mini-VTAB-C), comparison to Model Ratatouille, few-shot evaluation, and an alternative stock (Franca) ablation.

The proposed 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline is a fair, compute-matched comparison that isolates the specific benefit of souping across SSL runs rather than just benefiting from more training.

Self-Seasoning is a creative and practically useful extension that allows mixture-coefficient selection without any labels, which is shown to be competitive with labeled seasoning and to outperform full fine-tuning in low-data regimes (Fig. 4, Table 9).

The experiment inter-training on the (disjoint) test distribution for robustness is a clever and underexplored use case, yielding the largest reported gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C), and the paper is careful to distinguish inter-training on the test distribution from inter-training on the literal test samples.
weaknesses: Most reported gains are modest (often well under 1 percentage point, e.g., Table 1 IN-Val/IN-ReaL/IN-V2/IN-HR/IN-A columns, Table 4 natural/clean numbers), and no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere in the paper. Given the granularity of many differences (e.g., 79.41 vs 79.38 vs 79.34), it is hard to assess whether the claimed improvements are reliable rather than noise from a single training run per configuration.

The 'greedy search' and 'best ingredient' selection procedures are chosen by IN-Val accuracy and then evaluated on many other test sets simultaneously; combined with the lack of repeated trials, this raises some risk of favorable selection effects inflating the apparent advantage of Self-Soups over baselines on held-out shift sets.

The headline robustness gains (+3.5%/+7%) rely on having access to unlabeled data from the target/shifted distribution at training time, which is a meaningfully different (and more favorable) setting than the standard robustness evaluation assumption; this dependency is acknowledged in the limitations but somewhat downplayed in the abstract/intro framing.

mini-VTAB and mini-VTAB-C use only 1K-sample subsets of each of the 21 datasets' train/test splits, which likely adds substantial variance to the already-small observed differences, especially for small or imbalanced-class datasets (e.g., Retinopathy, Camelyon).

The method introduces additional inter-training stages, multiple SSL algorithms/hyperparameters, and larger search spaces; while the paper argues this is 'equal search/development cost' relative to the continued-SSL baseline, the real-world practical cost (multiple SSL pretraining runs per ingredient) relative to the size of the resulting gains is not deeply analyzed from a cost-benefit perspective, apart from the schematic discussion in Fig. 3.

LeJEPA, used in a key experiment (Fig. 2), is a contemporaneous/very recent method (cited as a 2025 preprint), making that particular comparison less grounded in established, independently-validated behavior.

The paper's five experimental settings, while broad, are somewhat disconnected from one another (different stocks, different numbers of ingredients, different inter-training lengths/hyperparameters chosen seemingly ad hoc per experiment), which makes it harder to build a unified, quantitatively predictive understanding of when and how much Self-Souping helps versus simpler baselines.
